fields.title: Whose needs you are actually gathering
fields.keyTakeaway: Requirements are not gathered from whoever asks loudest, but from whoever can stop the project and whoever will live with the result. Influence and interest are different axes, and they are confused most often.
fields.checkQuestion: The head of security never came to a meeting. Which quadrant will you put them in, and what will you do about it?
fields.blocks/0/text: The key question of this node: **what goals and problems exist in the company?** It arises because an internal product always has multiple stakeholders who want different things. The one who pays, the one who uses it, and the one who can veto it are usually three different people.
fields.blocks/1/text: Dispetcher is a fictional internal product for Surma, a transport company: 60 trucks, intercity freight, trip planning, and driver allocation. Dispatchers use it, the COO pays for it, and drivers and finance see the results. We will return to it in every lesson of this domain.
fields.blocks/2/text: **What happens if you do not answer this question.** You gather requirements from whoever writes to you most often. The product launches, and at acceptance, someone nobody thought about shows up with an objection that undoes half the work. Formally, they are right: nobody asked them.
fields.blocks/3/subtitle: Two axes, four quadrants, four different strategies
fields.blocks/3/items/0: **Influence**—whether a person can stop or turn back the project.
fields.blocks/3/items/1: **Interest**—how much the result changes their own work.
fields.blocks/3/items/2: **High influence + high interest**—work closely with them; they are co-authors of the solution.
fields.blocks/3/items/3: **High influence + low interest**—keep them informed briefly; their danger is that they show up late and out of nowhere.
fields.blocks/3/items/4: **Low influence + high interest**—the main source of requirements and future champions of the product.
fields.blocks/3/items/5: **Low influence + low interest**—observers; no need to spend time on them.
fields.blocks/4/text: The point of the matrix is not to sort people into boxes, but to acknowledge that **influence and interest are uncorrelated**. The most interested person often cannot decide anything, while the one who can learns about the product at the last minute—and breaks plans for that exact reason.
fields.blocks/5/text:
COO: high influence, medium interest. Pays, but doesn't micro-manage; cares only about vehicle downtime.
Dispatchers (4 people): low influence, maximum interest. They are in the product every day and know where it hurts.
Chief Accountant: high influence, low interest. Nobody remembered her—yet she is the one who accepts waybills at month-end and can reject the new format.
Drivers: zero influence, high interest, but nobody asks them because they don't sit in the office.

Before the matrix, the stakeholder list had two rows: COO and dispatchers.
fields.blocks/6/text: A person with high influence and low interest does not attend meetings or write in chat. You will hear their objection once—at the end, and it will cost more than all the others.
fields.blocks/6/title: Dangerous isn't the one who argues, but the one who stays silent
fields.blocks/7/text: The matrix describes people, not their tasks: it tells you whom to ask, but not what you will hear. It is static—interest grows as soon as the product touches someone's metrics. And it doesn't work as an excuse: "they have low influence" is not a reason to ignore a real problem.
